components.name:
The purpose of this model is to illustrate how information and control signals move within a modern connected vehicle, focusing on the relationships between infotainment systems, computing platforms, electronic control units (ECUs), and external networks. It captures how human interactions, onboard computing, and vehicle subsystems communicate to support entertainment, comfort, safety, and driving automation. The model is designed to help analyze security, privacy, and integration risks across hardware, software, and communication interfaces in a vehicle’s digital ecosystem.

The system structure is divided into several interconnected domains. The infotainment system forms the user-facing hub, handling inputs from the human driver or passengers through touch screens, rear screens, microphones, and connected devices such as mobile phones and tablets via Bluetooth or USB. These inputs are processed by controllers within the infotainment subsystem, which operates under an infotainment operating system that coordinates multimedia functions, communications, and environment settings. The onboard computer in the computing system acts as the vehicle’s core processing unit, linking infotainment features with vehicle control systems and managing overall logic, computation, and integration across multiple domains.

The CAN bus network connects the vehicle’s electronic control units, which handle critical and non-critical subsystems. These include the engine and powertrain ECU, transmission ECU, braking and safety ECU, body and comfort systems ECU, and advanced driver assistance ECU. Through this network, real-time operational data such as speed, torque, braking status, and environmental controls are transmitted between systems to support functions like adaptive cruise control, HVAC adjustments, traction control, and airbag deployment. The computing system ensures safe and prioritized communication between infotainment and the CAN bus without exposing sensitive control systems to unnecessary risk.

Application services in this model are distributed across the infotainment OS and the connected vehicle ecosystem. The infotainment OS manages entertainment, navigation, and connectivity, while vehicle ECUs handle safety, comfort, and automation features. The network components—Wi-Fi and GPS—extend the system beyond the vehicle, enabling over-the-air updates, telemetry, and navigation through communication with the vehicle manufacturer and internet data sources. GPS satellites provide location-based services, feeding into both navigation and advanced driver assistance functionalities.

The cloud components enable external data exchange, diagnostics, and updates. Wi-Fi connectivity links the vehicle to manufacturer systems for software updates, performance monitoring, and telemetry uploads, while internet data sources provide real-time traffic, mapping, and media services. These components allow for ongoing system optimization and remote servicing.

The modeling scope of this diagram focuses on logical data and control flows between human interfaces, vehicle computing systems, and external networks. It illustrates the trust boundaries between user-facing components, onboard computing, and vehicular control systems.

threats.name: Client-Side Injection
threats.description: Attackers exploit vulnerabilities by injecting malicious code (e.g., JavaScript, SQL queries) into the mobile app.

threats.name: Reverse Engineering
threats.description: Attackers decompile or reverse-engineer the mobile app to understand its functionality, extract sensitive data, or discover vulnerabilities.

threats.name: Insecure Communication with Third-Party Services
threats.description: Mobile apps often interact with third-party APIs or services, which may be insecure or malicious.

threats.name: Vulnerable and Outdated Components
threats.description: An attacker could target vulnerable and outdated components, such as libraries, frameworks, and other software modules, to execute various attacks.

threats.name: Broken access control
threats.description: An attacker could exploit broken access control to access unauthorized functionality and data, such as accessing other users' accounts, viewing sensitive files, modifying other users’ data, and changing access rights.

threats.name: Voice-assistant command injection
threats.description: Voice-recognition interfaces can be tricked by ultrasonic or hidden audio commands (so-called “silent speech attacks”). Attackers may issue commands to dial numbers, access data, or modify system settings. Privacy threats arise when assistants transmit voice data to third-party servers.

threats.name: Compromised mobile app integrations (Android Auto / CarPlay)
threats.description: When smartphones connect via Android Auto or Apple CarPlay, vulnerabilities in mobile apps or USB drivers can serve as attack vectors. Malware on the phone could exploit weak isolation between the mobile and infotainment environments. This creates a path for lateral movement into vehicle networks.

threats.name: Session Hijacking
threats.description: An attacker discovers/compromises the session management strategy and gains access to an object by impersonating another user or a service.

threats.name: Broken Authentication
threats.description: Attackers could target authentication mechanisms, potentially gaining complete control of other users' accounts, accessing their data, and performing actions on their behalf.

threats.name: Insecure Data Storage
threats.description: Sensitive data (like personal information, credentials, or financial data) stored insecurely on the device can be accessed by unauthorized parties if the device is lost, stolen, or compromised.

threats.name: Malicious Code and Malware
threats.description: Mobile devices can be infected with malware that can compromise apps, steal data, or perform unauthorized actions.

threats.name: Hijacked OTA (Over-the-Air) update mechanisms
threats.description: Compromised OTA servers or unverified firmware packages can inject malicious software into the infotainment unit. Without proper signature verification and secure boot, attackers can install persistent malware. This grants long-term control and surveillance capabilities.

threats.name: Cryptographic failure
threats.description: An attacker could exploit cryptographic failures to access sensitive data unprotected, such as credit card information, personal data, or business secrets.

threats.name: Insufficient Transport Layer Protection
threats.description: Data transmitted between the mobile app and server can be intercepted if not properly encrypted.

threats.name: Side-channel data leakage
threats.description: Sensitive data can be inadvertently exposed through logs, screenshots, or background apps.

threats.name: Exploiting unpatched software vulnerabilities
threats.description: Attackers may exploit outdated or unpatched software in the infotainment operating system to execute arbitrary code. Once compromised, they can gain control over system functions or pivot to other in-vehicle networks. This often occurs when OEMs delay security updates or use legacy components.

threats.name: Security Misconfiguration (Web and Mobile)
threats.description: An attacker could exploit security misconfigurations to gain unauthorized access or functionality. This could include unpatched flaws, unprotected files, and directories, or default accounts.

threats.name: Insecure Inter-Process Communication (IPC)
threats.description: Insecure communication between apps or components can be intercepted or manipulated.

threats.name: Weak Server-Side Controls
threats.description: Servers interacting with the mobile app may have vulnerabilities due to improper authentication, authorization, or input validation.

threats.name: Lateral movement to CAN or vehicle control networks
threats.description: If the infotainment system shares a bridge or gateway with the vehicle’s CAN bus, a compromise may spread to safety-critical ECUs. This allows attackers to manipulate braking, steering, or sensor systems indirectly. Network segmentation flaws greatly amplify this risk.

threats.name: Malicious USB device injection
threats.description: A malicious USB stick or device can deliver payloads when connected to the media or diagnostic port. These can exploit parsing vulnerabilities in file systems or firmware loaders. Such attacks are particularly dangerous because they often bypass network-based defenses.

threats.name: Data Disclosure
threats.description:
Excessively collecting, storing, processing, or sharing personal data. The data minimization principle is critical here: only the strictly necessary data should be collected or disclosed.

Data disclosure can be explicit, i.e., intended or designed by the system, or implicit, i.e., unintended or indirect (e.g., through metadata or derived from other data).

The focus is on four threat characteristics:

Unnecessary data types: this relates to the data type sensitivity, granularity, and encoding, which can be too detailed
Excessive data volume: this relates to the amount and frequency of the data processing and the number of involved data subjects, which can be too high
Unnecessary processing: this relates to the further data treatment analysis, propagation, or retention, which can be considered not strictly necessary
Excessive exposure: this relates to the different parties with whom the data is shared, which can be considered too much, and how widely accessible the data is

threats.name: Bluetooth exploitation
threats.description: Weak Bluetooth implementations or pairing protocols can allow attackers to eavesdrop, inject commands, or access internal data. Exploiting Bluetooth vulnerabilities may not require physical access if the vehicle’s pairing mode is active. Attackers can impersonate trusted devices or trigger DoS conditions.

threats.name: Unauthorized CAN message injection
threats.description: Attackers can inject forged messages onto the CAN bus to impersonate legitimate ECUs. Since the CAN protocol lacks authentication, other modules may accept and act on malicious commands. This can directly manipulate vehicle behavior, such as disabling brakes or spoofing sensor data.

threats.name: Key or credential leakage from ECUs
threats.description: Some ECUs store cryptographic keys or authentication tokens insecurely in flash or RAM. Physical attackers can extract these through chip-off or debugging interfaces. Once leaked, these secrets allow reprogramming, cloning, or remote unlocking of other vehicles.

threats.name: Replay attacks on CAN traffic
threats.description: Captured legitimate messages can be replayed at a later time to trigger vehicle actions without authorization. For example, replaying a door-unlock or engine-start command. CAN’s stateless design makes it difficult to distinguish old messages from current ones.

threats.name: ECU firmware manipulation or reflashing
threats.description: If attackers gain access to diagnostic ports or OTA update systems, they can overwrite ECU firmware. This may install persistent malware or modify control logic. Unsigned or poorly verified firmware updates make this attack feasible.

threats.name: ECU impersonation / spoofing
threats.description: A malicious device attached to the CAN network can masquerade as a legitimate ECU. It can send control commands or respond to queries to mislead other modules. Without message authentication, the vehicle cannot differentiate between genuine and fake ECUs.

threats.name: Memory corruption or buffer overflow in ECU software
threats.description: Bugs in ECU firmware parsers or network stacks can lead to memory corruption when malformed CAN or diagnostic packets are received. Attackers can exploit these vulnerabilities to execute arbitrary code. This is especially dangerous when firmware runs with high privilege.

threats.name: Bus flooding / Denial-of-service (DoS)
threats.description: Attackers can flood the CAN bus with high-priority frames, monopolizing bandwidth and preventing legitimate traffic. This can disable safety-critical systems or cause unpredictable ECU behavior. The system may appear frozen or enter a fail-safe mode.

threats.name: Exploiting insecure bootloaders
threats.description: If ECUs do not enforce secure boot, attackers can load modified or malicious firmware images. This can persist even after power cycles and evade standard diagnostics. Secure boot validation failure is a major vector for long-term compromise.

threats.name: Gateway or bridge compromise
threats.description: Modern vehicles use central gateways to isolate CAN subnets (powertrain, chassis, body). A compromised gateway ECU can bridge malicious messages across domains. This allows attackers to escalate from infotainment or telematics systems into safety-critical networks.

threats.name: Diagnostic interface exploitation (OBD-II, UDS)
threats.description: Standardized diagnostic protocols like UDS (Unified Diagnostic Services) allow access to memory, fault codes, and even firmware updates. If not properly restricted, attackers can use these interfaces to alter configurations or reprogram ECUs. Remote attacks are possible when the diagnostic stack is exposed via telematics or infotainment gateways.

threats.name: Engine & Powertrain ECU Overload / Destructive DoS
threats.description: An attacker who gains access to the powertrain CAN domain (via compromised gateway, telematics, OBD-II, or lateral movement) can flood the Engine Control Unit (ECU) with high-frequency or malformed control messages. By overwhelming the ECU’s processing capacity or suppressing critical sensor data (e.g., temperature, RPM, oil pressure), the attacker can induce incorrect engine behavior. This may disable safety limiters or cause the ECU to miss protective shutdown thresholds, allowing the engine to over-rev, overheat, or run without proper fuel/air balance, leading to catastrophic mechanical failure (“engine blowout”) or permanent damage.

threats.name: Braking & Safety ECU Command Suppression / Safety System Disablement
threats.description: An attacker with access to the vehicle’s internal networks (through compromised infotainment, telematics, OBD-II, or a breached gateway ECU) can inject spoofed or high-priority CAN frames that override or suppress legitimate braking, ABS, ESC, or airbag control messages. Because many braking and safety ECUs rely on unauthenticated, real-time CAN traffic, the attacker can block critical sensor inputs, disable actuator commands, or send false states that trick the system into thinking conditions are normal. This can result in brakes failing to engage, airbags failing to deploy during a crash, or safety interventions (ABS/ESC) being silently disabled. The outcome is direct compromise of occupant safety with high risk of injury or fatality.

threats.name: Exploiting legacy or unsupported firmware
threats.description: Vehicles often run outdated infotainment firmware that no longer receives patches. Attackers can use known exploits to compromise such systems indefinitely. These vulnerabilities persist across multiple model years, creating systemic risk.

threats.name: ADAS Sensor Manipulation / Assistance System Degradation
threats.description: An attacker who compromises vehicle networks or ADAS sensor inputs (camera, radar, ultrasonic, or LiDAR) can disrupt or falsify data fed into the Advanced Driver Assistance ECU. By injecting spoofed CAN messages, jamming or blinding sensors, or suppressing perception data, the attacker can cause lane-keeping systems to drift, adaptive cruise control to misjudge distance, or parking assistance to fail. Since ADAS depends on real-time, accurate sensor fusion, these manipulations can disable lane guidance, create unsafe following behavior, or cause the ECU to ignore obstacles. In extreme cases, the system may apply incorrect steering, braking, or acceleration, putting occupants and bystanders at risk.

mitigations.name: Validate User Input
mitigations.description: Implement strict input validation to ensure user-provided data adheres to expected formats, types, and constraints. Reject or sanitize any input that does not meet these criteria to prevent potential security vulnerabilities such as injection attacks or unauthorized access.
mitigations.question: Are you validating all user input against strict criteria?
mitigations.consideration:
- Use whitelisting for acceptable input formats and values.
- Implement regular expressions to enforce input patterns.
- Limit input length to mitigate buffer overflow risks.
- Validate data types explicitly
- Employ context-aware encoding for output.
-Add rate limiting to block brute-force input
- Use security libraries or frameworks with built-in validation.
- Log and monitor invalid input for analysis.
mitigations.explanation: Input validation ensures user data is clean, expected, and secure before processing. Strong validation prevents injection, overflow, and brute-force attacks. Input rules should align with business logic, and validation must happen both client- and server-side. Monitoring rejected inputs can help identify attack patterns and improve defenses over time.
mitigations.example:
- Joi (Node.js): Define and enforce input schemas using clear syntax
- Validator.js: Validate and sanitize strings (e.g., emails, URLs)
- Express-validator: Middleware for input validation in Express apps
- Yup (JavaScript/TypeScript): Schema validation for form inputs
- OWASP ESAPI: Java library for input validation and encoding

mitigations.name: Implement Parameterization
mitigations.description: Use parameterized queries and prepared statements to enforce strict separation of code and data in database and OS operations, preventing injection attacks. Ensure input values are bound to placeholders rather than concatenated into code strings.
mitigations.question: Are parameterized queries used for all database and OS operations to prevent injection by separating code from data?
mitigations.consideration:
- Enforce use of parameterized APIs or libraries for all command and database operations.
- Audit codebases to identify and eliminate unsafe string concatenation.
- Validate all input values before binding them to parameters.
- Ensure consistent use of prepared statements in both backend and frontend frameworks.
- Regularly test parameter handling through code reviews and security audits.
mitigations.explanation: Parameterization works by clearly separating user input from the command or query structure. Instead of injecting input directly into commands, parameters are used as placeholders, which prevents injection attacks. This technique ensures inputs are interpreted strictly as data, not executable code. Regular audits and validations help maintain its effectiveness, especially in preventing OS and database-level injection threats.
mitigations.example:
- For OS Command Injection, libraries like Apache Commons Exec and Python's subprocess module provide methods to safely execute commands with parameters.
- In Python, use the subprocess.run(["cmd", param]) pattern.
- In Java, use PreparedStatement to bind variables in SQL queries.
- In web apps, frameworks like React escape inputs in templates, and libraries like DOMPurify sanitize HTML.
- Use ORMs like SQLAlchemy or Entity Framework to enforce parameterization automatically.

mitigations.name: Change default credentials immediately
mitigations.description: Change all default credentials for admin and user accounts immediately. Implement strong, unique passwords for each account to prevent unauthorized access.
mitigations.question: Have all default credentials been replaced with strong, unique passwords?
mitigations.consideration:
- Identify all accounts using factory-default credentials
- Change default usernames and passwords during initial setup
- Use tools or scripts to enforce password changes upon first login
- Remove or disable default accounts that are not needed
- Apply secure, unique passwords when replacing default credentials
- Verify that no systems are deployed with hardcoded or unchanged defaults
mitigations.explanation: Default credentials are widely known and often exploited in attacks. Systems should enforce immediate credential changes upon deployment or initial login. All default admin and user accounts must be reviewed and updated with strong, unique passwords. Where possible, default accounts should be removed entirely. Automating detection and enforcement of credential changes reduces risk and helps prevent unauthorized access due to overlooked defaults.
mitigations.example:
- OS hardening scripts (e.g., Ansible, PowerShell DSC): Automate credential resets on first boot
- AWS IAM Access Analyzer: Flags accounts using default or overly permissive credentials
- Dockerfile best practices: Recommend overriding default credentials at container build time
- OpenVAS / Nessus: Detect systems using known default credentials during scans

mitigations.name: Implement Code Obfuscation
mitigations.description: Use code obfuscation techniques to make your mobile app's source and machine code difficult to interpret.
mitigations.question: Is code obfuscation applied to make your app’s source and machine code difficult to reverse-engineer?
mitigations.consideration:
- Choose robust obfuscation tools that are regularly updated to counter new reverse engineering techniques.
- Combine obfuscation with other security measures, such as encryption and secure coding practices, for layered protection.
- Regularly evaluate the effectiveness of obfuscation methods against current reverse engineering tools.
- Educate developers on the importance of secure coding and obfuscation practices.
mitigations.explanation: Code obfuscation transforms readable source code into a harder-to-understand version without changing its behavior. This makes reverse engineering more difficult. It typically includes renaming identifiers, altering control flow, and inserting dummy code. Automated build tools help integrate obfuscation into development pipelines, and regular updates ensure resistance to evolving analysis methods.
mitigations.example:
- ProGuard: A tool for Android that shrinks, optimizes, and obfuscates code.
- DexGuard: An advanced version of ProGuard with extra Android security.
- R8: A modern code shrinker and obfuscator for Android apps.
- ConfuserEx: An open-source .NET obfuscator.
- JavaGuard: A Java obfuscator to prevent reverse engineering.
- DashO: A commercial tool for Java and Android with advanced obfuscation.

mitigations.name: Develop a comprehensive threat model
mitigations.description: Identify and evaluate potential threats to systems by analyzing assets, attack surfaces, and vulnerabilities. Develop a structured threat model to understand how attackers could exploit weaknesses and to prioritize risks. Use this model to inform future security design and decision-making.
mitigations.question: Have you developed a comprehensive threat model for your systems?
mitigations.consideration:
- Identify assets, users, and data flows
- Map attack surfaces and trust boundaries
- Enumerate threats using frameworks like STRIDE or MITRE ATT&CK
- Assess likelihood and impact for risk prioritization
- Involve cross-functional teams (security, dev, ops)
- Update the model regularly to reflect system changes
mitigations.explanation: Threat modeling involves identifying system assets, mapping how data flows between components, and evaluating how attackers might exploit vulnerabilities. Teams use frameworks like STRIDE to classify threats and assess risks. The model guides secure design and helps prioritize mitigations based on potential impact.
mitigations.example:
- Devici for structured threat modeling and risk analysis
- SD Elements (SDE) for integrating threat modeling into secure development workflows
- MITRE ATT&CK for identifying and mapping adversary techniques
- Draw.io or Lucidchart for visualizing system architecture and data flow

mitigations.name: Encrypt all data in transit using secure protocols.
mitigations.description: Encrypt all data in transit using current, secure communication protocols such as TLS 1.3. Ensure all services and APIs are authenticated and data is encrypted between endpoints to protect against interception and tampering. Validate implementation against cryptographic best practices, and avoid deprecated or insecure protocols. Regularly review and update configurations to maintain data integrity and confidentiality.
mitigations.question: Is all data in transit encrypted using secure protocols like TLS 1.3?
mitigations.consideration:
- Use strong, modern encryption protocols (e.g., TLS 1.3) and secure cipher suites.
- Implement certificate pinning to protect against man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks.
- Ensure third-party libraries and dependencies related to cryptography are kept up to date.
- Conduct regular audits and penetration tests to verify secure implementation of encryption in transit.
- Use mutual TLS (mTLS) where appropriate to authenticate both client and server.
mitigations.explanation: Securing data in transit involves encrypting all communications between clients, servers, and third-party systems using modern protocols like TLS 1.3. Certificate pinning strengthens MITM defenses, while mutual TLS ensures both endpoints are authenticated. Keeping libraries updated prevents the use of known-vulnerable cryptographic methods. Regular testing and validation confirm correct implementation and allow prompt remediation of weaknesses in encrypted communication paths.
mitigations.example:
- TLS 1.3 for end-to-end encrypted communication
- HTTPS for secure web traffic
- Mutual TLS (mTLS) for API authentication
- Certificate pinning in mobile apps
- OpenSSL for implementing strong cryptographic protocols
- Cloudflare WAF to inspect and secure encrypted traffic
- VPNs for encrypted connections to external systems

mitigations.name: Source trusted libraries and packages
mitigations.description: Source components exclusively from official repositories. Regularly audit and update libraries and frameworks to ensure they are maintained and free from vulnerabilities.
mitigations.question: Are all your libraries sourced from official and trusted repositories?
mitigations.consideration:
- Verify the integrity of libraries using checksums or digital signatures
- Use official repositories with active community and vendor support
- Monitor security advisories for components in use
- Automate dependency management and update tracking
- Establish a process for deprecating and replacing outdated libraries
- Limit or review use of third-party libraries from unknown or unverified sources
mitigations.explanation: Implement tools that source libraries from trusted repositories and verify integrity using digital signatures or checksums. Regular audits should identify outdated or risky components. Automate alerts for security advisories and enforce policies for deprecating unsupported libraries. Dependency managers help track third-party usage and reduce reliance on unverified sources, promoting safe and reliable software composition.
mitigations.example:
- npm: Sources packages from the official Node registry and includes audit tools
- Maven: Manages Java dependencies from Maven Central with version control
- Composer: Pulls PHP libraries from Packagist and includes security advisories
- GitHub Dependabot: Automates updates and flags vulnerable packages
- Snyk: Scans open-source libraries and recommends secure alternatives
- JFrog Artifactory: Hosts trusted internal and third-party components securely

mitigations.name: Eliminate unused dependencies
mitigations.description: Remove all unused dependencies and features from your software components to reduce potential attack surfaces. Regularly audit and update remaining components to ensure they are current and secure.
mitigations.question: Are all unused dependencies removed and regularly audited in your software?
mitigations.consideration:
- Implement automated tools to identify and remove unused dependencies.
- Establish a regular schedule for dependency audits and updates.
- Utilize dependency management tools to track versions and vulnerabilities.
- Educate developers on the risks of excessive dependencies.
- Promote minimalistic, well-maintained libraries to reduce complexity.
mitigations.explanation: Eliminating unused dependencies reduces the attack surface by removing unnecessary code and libraries. Automated tools can scan for unused components during builds, while regular audits ensure outdated or insecure packages are addressed. Dependency managers help track versions and vulnerabilities, and ongoing monitoring promotes secure, lean development practices.
mitigations.example:
- npm audit: Identifies and reports vulnerabilities in Node.js dependencies.
- Bundler: A Ruby tool to manage and clean unused gems.
- Gradle: Supports removal of unused Java dependencies during builds.
- Dependabot: Automatically updates and helps clean unused GitHub dependencies.
- SonarQube: Detects unused code and libraries in various languages.
- Depcheck: Scans JavaScript projects for unused or missing dependencies.

mitigations.name: Conduct Software Composition Analysis
mitigations.description: Regularly assess and update all software components, libraries, and frameworks to the latest secure versions. Implement automated checks for vulnerabilities and ensure all software updates are verified for integrity before deployment.
mitigations.question: Are you regularly assessing and updating all software components for security to detect and patch known vulnerabilities?
mitigations.consideration:
- Use SCA tools to detect vulnerable third-party components.
- Define policies for managing component updates and acceptable license types.
- Integrate SCA into CI/CD pipelines to trigger checks automatically.
- Track software bill of materials (SBOM) to improve visibility of open-source use.
- Educate developers on selecting well-maintained, secure libraries.
- Verify software integrity using cryptographic signatures when available.
mitigations.explanation: Software Composition Analysis (SCA) identifies known vulnerabilities in third-party libraries and open-source components. By integrating SCA into the CI/CD pipeline, organizations can detect risks early and enforce policies for safe and compliant component use. SCA tools help maintain visibility over software supply chains and alert teams to security, license, or integrity concerns, enabling timely updates and reducing risk.
mitigations.example:
- Snyk: Scans open-source dependencies for vulnerabilities and license risks.
- OWASP Dependency-Check: Identifies known vulnerable components in Java and .NET.
- GitHub Dependabot: Scans for outdated libraries and creates update pull requests.
- Docker Content Trust: Verifies container image integrity using digital signatures.
- Veracode SCA: Detects and manages risks in third-party libraries.
- JFrog Xray: Analyzes binaries and enforces open-source policies.

mitigations.name: Enforce record ownership in models
mitigations.description: Implement strict ownership checks in your data models to ensure users can only access their own records. Validate user permissions at the model level to prevent unauthorized access to functionality and data.
mitigations.question: Are ownership checks enforced in data models to ensure users can only access their own records based on validated permissions?
mitigations.consideration:
- Apply ownership checks at all access layers, including APIs, services, and UI.
- Use unique user identifiers to associate records with owners.
- Employ RBAC to define and enforce access boundaries based on ownership.
- Log access attempts and monitor for violations or anomalies.
- Regularly review access rules to reflect changes in user roles or system structure.
- Provide secure coding guidelines to help developers implement consistent ownership checks.
mitigations.explanation: Record ownership enforcement involves linking each data entry to a specific user and validating ownership before granting access. This check should be implemented at the model or middleware level to ensure it applies regardless of how data is accessed. Role-based access controls (RBAC) can refine permissions to only allow users to interact with their own records. Ownership checks must be applied consistently across all components, with logging and alerting to detect unauthorized access attempts.
mitigations.example:
- AWS IAM: Enables permissions based on ownership of specific resources.
- OAuth 2.0: Scopes access tokens to user-specific data, enforcing ownership.
- Django: Uses mixins and decorators to restrict views to owner’s records.
- Microsoft Azure AD: Supports RBAC to enforce access rules at resource levels.
- Spring Security: Supports annotations for method-level ownership checks in Java apps.

mitigations.name: Deny Access by Default
mitigations.description: Enforce a deny-by-default access control policy, where no user, system, or plugin is granted access unless explicitly allowed by defined rules. Default behavior should reject all requests until specific permissions are granted through access policies or allow-lists.
mitigations.question: Is your access control policy configured to deny all access by default unless explicitly permitted by defined rules?
mitigations.consideration:
- Define explicit allow-lists for all actions, users, services, and data access.
- Configure default access controls to deny any request unless explicitly authorized.
- Ensure all new plugins, APIs, and user roles are evaluated for access restrictions before deployment.
- Review access control configurations regularly to ensure no implicit permissions exist.
- Enforce access policies through infrastructure-as-code or configuration management to prevent misconfigurations.
mitigations.explanation: Deny-by-default policies ensure that access is never assumed or open by default. Instead, each access request must meet pre-approved conditions before being granted. This limits the potential attack surface and prevents unauthorized interactions. By configuring allow-lists and enforcing explicit permissions at every layer—from API gateways to internal services, organizations prevent unintended access. Regular audits help detect and remove outdated or overly permissive rules.
mitigations.example:
- AWS IAM: IAM policies can be configured to deny all access unless specifically allowed via policies.
- Google Cloud IAM uses allow-based roles where no access is granted until explicitly permitted.
- API Gateways: Only routes explicitly defined in the gateway are reachable; others are denied by default.
- Azure Resource Manager enforces deny-by-default behavior in RBAC assignments.
- Kubernetes Network Policies deny all pod-to-pod communication by default unless allow-rules are defined.

mitigations.name: Implement Access Control Measures
mitigations.description: Implement robust access control mechanisms to validate and authorize each entity's actions within the system. Ensure that permissions are strictly enforced to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive data and functionality. Regularly review and update access controls to address vulnerabilities and adhere to the principle of least privilege.
mitigations.question: Are access controls strictly enforced and regularly reviewed?
mitigations.consideration:
- Define clear access policies based on job responsibilities and data sensitivity
- Use least privilege as a default for all roles and permissions
- Separate duties across roles to reduce risk from over-privileged accounts
- Review and update access rights regularly, especially after role changes
- Apply fine-grained access control at the resource, function, and data level
mitigations.explanation: Access control ensures users and systems only access what they need based on roles and responsibilities. By applying least privilege and separating duties, organizations reduce the risk of abuse or error. Fine-grained controls restrict access to specific data or functions, and regular reviews ensure permissions stay aligned with evolving roles.
mitigations.example:
- AWS IAM / Azure RBAC: Define and manage granular role-based access
- Okta / Keycloak: Centralize user role management and access policies
- OPA (Open Policy Agent): Enforce fine-grained access at the application level
- GitLab / GitHub Roles: Control project and repository access by role
- GCP IAM Conditions: Apply attribute-based access rules for resources

mitigations.name: Implement access control mechanisms
mitigations.description: Implement access control mechanisms consistently across the application to ensure that every user action is explicitly authorized. Validate permissions at all entry points, including API endpoints, services, and internal functions, to prevent unauthorized access to data and functionality.
mitigations.question: Are access control mechanisms enforced at all entry points in your app?
mitigations.consideration:
- Define and document a unified access control strategy for all system components.
- Enforce access control at multiple layers (API gateway, backend services, databases).
- Use centralized policy engines (e.g., RBAC or ABAC) to apply consistent rules.
- Perform static and dynamic testing to identify endpoints lacking access checks.
- Monitor access patterns and log unauthorized attempts for analysis.
- Train developers to apply consistent authorization checks during development.
mitigations.explanation: Consistent access control ensures that no part of the application allows unauthorized access due to missing or inconsistent permission checks. Implementing centralized enforcement mechanisms like RBAC or ABAC ensures rules are uniformly applied across all endpoints and services. Security tools should verify that access control policies are in place at every interaction point. Logging, audits, and testing tools help maintain coverage and identify violations over time.
mitigations.example:
- AWS IAM for managing user permissions and roles.
- OAuth 2.0 for delegated access control in APIs, ensuring users can only access resources they are authorized to.
- API Gateway services (e.g., Amazon API Gateway, Azure API Management) that enforce access policies at the function level.
- Open Policy Agent (OPA) for implementing fine-grained access control based on policies.
- Role-based access control features in platforms like Microsoft Azure Active Directory.

mitigations.name: User-Verified Actions and Robust Command Authentication
mitigations.description: Require explicit user verification (wake word, proximity checks, or confirmation prompts) for sensitive actions such as dialing, data access, and system changes, and harden the voice stack against ultrasonic/inaudible patterns by filtering inaudible frequencies and enforcing human-audible command characteristics.

mitigations.name: Privacy-Respecting Voice Processing and Restricted Data Exposure
mitigations.description: Minimize voice data sent to third-party servers by preferring on-device processing where possible, encrypt all transmitted audio, and restrict the assistant’s access to contacts, messages, and vehicle/system controls to least-privilege scopes, reducing both command-abuse impact and privacy leakage if voice traffic is intercepted or misused.

mitigations.name: Strict Isolation and Sandboxing Between Mobile and Infotainment Domains
mitigations.description: Enforce hardened isolation between Android Auto / CarPlay processes and the infotainment system, using sandboxing, containerization, and restricted IPC so connected mobile apps cannot access privileged interfaces or pivot into vehicle-side services, even if the phone is compromised.

mitigations.name: Controlled USB / Wireless Interfaces With Policy Enforcement and Threat Detection
mitigations.description: Restrict Android Auto / CarPlay interfaces to approved protocols and validated message types, apply strict filtering at the USB/wireless ingress point, and monitor for anomalous behavior from connected devices to prevent malware or tampered apps from abusing integration channels to reach in-vehicle networks.

mitigations.name: Implement strong authentication with 2FA or MFA.
mitigations.description: Implement Two-Factor Authentication (2FA) or Multi-Factor Authentication (MFA) to enhance identity verification for all users.
mitigations.question: Is 2FA or MFA enforced for all user logins in your system?
mitigations.consideration:
- Select authentication methods that combine at least two distinct factors (e.g., password + TOTP or hardware token)
- Require biometric factors where possible for enhanced security.
- Support widely adopted authenticators like TOTP apps or FIDO2 devices
- Enforce MFA for all users, especially for privileged accounts
- Ensure fallback mechanisms are secure and limited
mitigations.explanation: Strong authentication with 2FA or MFA uses two or more factors—like passwords and TOTP apps or hardware tokens—to verify user identity. Even if a password is compromised, a second factor helps prevent unauthorized access. MFA should be enforced across all login flows, including admin panels and APIs, to reduce the risk of account takeover and credential-based attacks.
mitigations.example:
- Google / Microsoft Authenticator: TOTP apps for 2FA
- YubiKey / SoloKey: Hardware tokens using FIDO2/U2F
- Duo Security: Enterprise MFA with multiple factor types
- GitHub / AWS / Salesforce: Offer built-in MFA enforcement
- Authy: Cross-device TOTP support with cloud sync

mitigations.name: Secure Service Token Management
mitigations.description: Implement secure generation, distribution, and storage protocols for service tokens used by Non-Person Entities. Ensure tokens are generated with strong cryptographic methods, distributed through secure channels, and stored in a protected environment to prevent unauthorized access and session hijacking.
mitigations.question: Are you using secure methods for generating and storing service tokens?
mitigations.consideration:
- Use short-lived tokens to limit the window of opportunity for an attacker.
- Implement token revocation mechanisms to invalidate compromised tokens immediately.
- Employ secure transport protocols (e.g., TLS) for token transmission.
- Regularly rotate tokens and keys to enhance security.
- Monitor and log token usage for anomaly detection.
- Apply strict access controls to token storage locations.
- Use multi-factor authentication to further secure token access.
mitigations.explanation: Tokens are generated using strong cryptographic algorithms, ensuring randomness and unpredictability. TSecure token handling reduces the risk of interception, misuse, or privilege escalation. Enforcing strict token lifecycles, transmission protections, and anomaly detection enhances resilience against session hijacking and unauthorized access.
mitigations.example:
Examples of technology that implement secure service token management include:
- OAuth 2.0 for authorization, which uses access tokens with expiration times
- JSON Web Tokens (JWT) for secure token generation and transmission
- AWS Security Token Service (STS) for temporary security credentials.

Tools like HashiCorp Vault for secure storage and management of tokens, and API gateways that enforce token validation and revocation policies are also relevant.

mitigations.description: Encrypt all sensitive data both in transit and at rest to protect it from unauthorized access. Implement strong encryption protocols for data flows crossing trust boundaries and ensure that sensitive information is stored securely using encryption methods that meet industry standards.
mitigations.question: Is all sensitive data encrypted in transit and at rest using strong protocols?
mitigations.consideration:
- Use strong encryption protocols (e.g., TLS 1.2+, AES-256) and avoid weak or outdated algorithms
- Encrypt data stored on disks, databases, and backups
- Apply encryption to data in transit across internal and external networks
- Ensure encryption is enabled by default in systems handling sensitive data
- Ensure encryption keys are securely managed and rotated regularly
mitigations.explanation: Sensitive data should be encrypted both at rest and in transit using strong protocols like AES-256 and TLS 1.2+. Encryption must be applied to all data crossing trust boundaries, such as between services or across networks. Keys should be stored securely and rotated regularly. Avoid weak algorithms and ensure encryption settings follow industry best practices by default.
mitigations.example:
- AES (Advanced Encryption Standard) for encrypting data at rest
- TLS (Transport Layer Security) for securing data in transit
- AWS Key Management Service (KMS) for secure key management
- Microsoft Azure Disk Encryption for encrypting virtual machine disks
- VeraCrypt for creating encrypted containers for sensitive files
- BitLocker for encrypting entire drives on Windows devices

mitigations.name: Secure credential recovery endpoints
mitigations.description: Implement strong security measures for credential recovery endpoints, including rate limiting, CAPTCHA, and multi-factor authentication. Ensure that recovery processes verify user identity rigorously and log all recovery attempts for monitoring and auditing.
mitigations.question: Are credential recovery endpoints protected with MFA, CAPTCHA, rate limiting, and identity verification with full logging?
mitigations.consideration:
- Ensure recovery links expire after a short duration to prevent misuse.
- Implement email or SMS verification for any changes to recovery information.
- Use unique, unpredictable tokens for recovery processes to prevent enumeration attacks.
- Regularly review and update recovery procedures to address emerging threats.
- Educate users on recognizing phishing attempts related to recovery processes.
mitigations.explanation: Credential recovery endpoints must enforce secure practices to prevent abuse. Recovery links should expire quickly to reduce the risk of reuse. Each recovery attempt should generate a unique, unpredictable token to prevent guessing or enumeration. Any change to recovery information should trigger email or SMS-based verification. Regular reviews ensure recovery workflows stay updated, while user training helps prevent phishing and social engineering attacks.
mitigations.example:
- Google Account Recovery: Uses MFA and token-based verification with expiration
- Authy: Sends SMS codes for recovery verification
- LastPass: Implements CAPTCHA, rate limiting, and email verification for changes
- Okta: Provides secure, customizable identity recovery workflows
- Microsoft Azure AD: Offers advanced recovery protections, including token expiration
- Duo Security: Supports multi-factor recovery verification with audit logging

mitigations.name: Map all authentication flows
mitigations.description: Identify and document all authentication flows across the system, including APIs, web, and mobile entry points. Include methods used (e.g., OAuth, SAML), token generation and expiration practices, and secure password storage. Regularly review and update this documentation to mitigate risks from broken or outdated authentication mechanisms.
mitigations.question: Have you documented all authentication flows in your system?
mitigations.consideration:
- Identify all entry points where authentication occurs, including APIs, web apps, and mobile platforms.
- Document the methods used for authentication and how credentials or tokens are validated.
- Include token expiration policies, refresh flows, and storage mechanisms.
- Verify password storage practices use secure hashing algorithms.
- Update the documentation regularly to reflect system changes or new access points.
- Involve relevant teams to validate completeness and accuracy
mitigations.explanation: Mapping authentication flows is essential to identify hidden entry points that could be exploited by attackers. Without a full inventory, it's easy to overlook outdated, duplicated, or misconfigured flows that increase the risk of credential misuse or session hijacking. A clear map improves visibility, simplifies risk analysis, and supports more effective access control and incident response planning.
mitigations.example:
- Use Postman + Auth logs (e.g., CloudTrail, SIEM) to manually trace real authentication journeys.
- Use IAM platforms to visualize configured flows.
- Use burp/ZAP to catch any hidden or forgotten endpoints during red teaming.

mitigations.name: Deploy anti-brute force protections
mitigations.description: Implement anti-brute force protections at all authentication endpoints to prevent unauthorized access. This includes account lockout policies, rate limiting, and CAPTCHA challenges after a specified number of failed login attempts.
mitigations.question: Are all authentication endpoints protected against brute-force attacks?
mitigations.consideration:
- Implement account lockout policies to temporarily disable accounts after failed login attempts
- Apply rate limiting to restrict repeated login attempts from the same source within a short timeframe
- Use CAPTCHA challenges after multiple failed attempts to block automated attacks
- Implement IP blacklisting for persistent attackers
- Monitor and log login attempts for suspicious patterns
- Test the effectiveness of protections through simulated attacks
mitigations.explanation: To defend against brute-force attacks, authentication endpoints must enforce layered protections. Account lockout policies temporarily disable access after repeated failures, while rate limiting restricts login attempts in a short timeframe. CAPTCHA challenges stop automated tools, and IP blacklisting blocks persistent attackers. Logging and regular testing ensure these controls remain effective against evolving threats.
mitigations.example:
- Cloudflare Bot Management: Enforces rate limiting and CAPTCHA after failed attempts
- Google reCAPTCHA: Blocks automated login attempts using challenge-response
- AWS WAF: Supports IP-based login throttling and blocking rules
- Fail2Ban: Analyzes logs and blacklists IPs after repeated failures
- Okta: Implements lockout policies and multi-layer login defenses
- Microsoft Azure AD: Provides account lockout, CAPTCHA, and adaptive risk-based controls

mitigations.description: Only download apps and files from reputable and verified sources to minimize the risk of malware infections.
mitigations.question: Are all apps and files downloaded exclusively from reputable and verified sources?
mitigations.consideration:
- Verify the source of apps and files before downloading, ensuring they originate from official stores or trusted vendors.
- Avoid third-party app stores and unknown websites.
- Check developer reputation, app reviews, and download counts.
- Confirm apps are signed and validated by the platform’s security mechanisms.
- Educate users to avoid pirated or cracked apps.
mitigations.explanation: Downloading only from trusted sources minimizes exposure to malicious software. Verified app stores use vetting mechanisms such as code reviews, digital signatures, and reputation systems to ensure authenticity and safety. Avoiding unofficial or pirated sources helps prevent malware infections, credential theft, and unauthorized data access.

mitigations.description: Require all OTA update packages to be cryptographically signed by OEM-trusted keys and validated on-device before installation, and pair this with secure boot so only verified firmware can execute, preventing attackers from injecting malicious or altered update images into the infotainment unit.

mitigations.description: Protect OTA servers, APIs, and distribution pipelines using strong authentication, encrypted channels, role-based access, and continuous integrity monitoring, ensuring attackers cannot compromise backend systems or spoof update sources to push unauthorized or persistent malware to vehicles.

mitigations.description: Classify data based on its sensitivity level (such as public, internal, confidential, or restricted) and apply appropriate controls for each category. This ensures that sensitive information is handled securely, meets compliance requirements, and is protected from unauthorized access or disclosure.
mitigations.question: Do you classify data based on its sensitivity level?
mitigations.consideration:
- Define clear classification tiers based on regulatory, legal, and business risk factors.
- Train personnel to recognize and handle each classification level correctly.
- Use automated tools to detect, label, and tag sensitive data across systems.
- Enforce different access control policies and encryption requirements per data class.
- Review and update classification schemes regularly based on evolving risks.
- Monitor access to sensitive data and generate alerts on anomalous activity.
mitigations.explanation: Data classification involves identifying and labeling information based on its sensitivity and risk level. This process enables organizations to apply the correct security controls to different types of data, such as encryption, access restrictions, and audit logging. Automated classification tools streamline enforcement by tagging sensitive information in real time. Ongoing monitoring and access reviews help detect misuse and support compliance obligations.

- Microsoft Information Protection for tagging and access control
- AWS Macie for discovering and labeling sensitive data in cloud storage
- VeraCrypt for encrypting sensitive files

- IBM Guardium for monitoring access to protected data

mitigations.description: Encrypt all data in transit using current, secure communication protocols such as TLS 1.3. Ensure all services and APIs are authenticated and data is encrypted between endpoints to protect against interception and tampering. Validate implementation against cryptographic best practices, and avoid deprecated or insecure protocols. Regularly review and update configurations to maintain data integrity and confidentiality.
mitigations.question: Is all data in transit encrypted using secure protocols like TLS 1.3?
mitigations.consideration:
- Use strong, modern encryption protocols (e.g., TLS 1.3) and secure cipher suites.
- Implement certificate pinning to protect against man-in-the-middle (MITM) attacks.
- Ensure third-party libraries and dependencies related to cryptography are kept up to date.
- Conduct regular audits and penetration tests to verify secure implementation of encryption in transit.
- Use mutual TLS (mTLS) where appropriate to authenticate both client and server.
mitigations.explanation: Securing data in transit involves encrypting all communications between clients, servers, and third-party systems using modern protocols like TLS 1.3. Certificate pinning strengthens MITM defenses, while mutual TLS ensures both endpoints are authenticated. Keeping libraries updated prevents the use of known-vulnerable cryptographic methods. Regular testing and validation confirm correct implementation and allow prompt remediation of weaknesses in encrypted communication paths.
mitigations.example:
- TLS 1.3 for end-to-end encrypted communication
- HTTPS for secure web traffic
- Mutual TLS (mTLS) for API authentication
- Certificate pinning in mobile apps
- OpenSSL for implementing strong cryptographic protocols
- Cloudflare WAF to inspect and secure encrypted traffic
- VPNs for encrypted connections to external systems

mitigations.name: Implement up-to-date encryption standards
mitigations.description: Apply the latest industry-approved encryption standards to protect sensitive data. Ensure cryptographic algorithms, protocols, and key management practices are regularly updated to mitigate emerging threats and comply with evolving security requirements.
mitigations.question: Are current industry-approved encryption standards used and regularly updated for sensitive data?
mitigations.consideration:
- Periodically assess encryption configurations to ensure compliance with current standards (e.g., NIST, ISO).
- Replace outdated algorithms (e.g., SHA-1, RSA-1024) with modern, secure alternatives (e.g., AES-256, SHA-3, ECC).
- Enforce key rotation schedules and ensure use of strong, unique keys.
- Monitor regulatory and vendor guidance for updates to approved encryption protocols.
- Train developers on proper use of cryptographic libraries and deprecation timelines.
mitigations.explanation: Keeping encryption mechanisms up to date requires continuous monitoring of cryptographic standards and replacing deprecated algorithms. This includes migrating from older protocols like TLS 1.1 to secure versions like TLS 1.3, using secure key lengths, and leveraging services that automatically adopt current best practices. Up-to-date encryption strengthens resilience against known exploits and ensures compliance with regulatory frameworks such as GDPR, HIPAA, or PCI-DSS.

- AWS KMS: Supports AES-256 and automatic key rotation.
- Azure Key Vault: Uses FIPS 140-2 validated modules.
- Google Cloud Encryption: Enforces TLS 1.3, supports customer-managed keys.
- OpenSSL 3.x: Includes modern cipher suites.
- Cloudflare: Uses TLS 1.3 for secure web traffic.
- Apple CryptoKit: Offers current encryption APIs for iOS/macOS.

Implement controls to prevent unauthorized access to logs and related data.
mitigations.question: Are logging configurations audited to ensure completeness, accuracy, no sensitive data exposure?
mitigations.consideration:
- Define logging levels clearly to distinguish between critical, warning, and informational events.
- Implement log rotation and retention policies to manage log size and ensure timely review.
- Use encryption for logs, especially those containing sensitive information, to prevent unauthorized access.
- Regularly train staff on logging best practices and the importance of data protection.
- Establish incident response protocols for when logging anomalies are detected.
mitigations.explanation: The system captures events based on defined logging levels, ensuring critical incidents are logged with high priority. Logs are structured to separate sensitive data from general information, utilizing data masking techniques. Logs are encrypted during transmission and storage. Automated tools analyze logs for anomalies, and alerts are generated for suspicious activities. Log access is restricted to authorized personnel only, with regular audits to ensure compliance and effectiveness.

mitigations.name: Regular, Secure, and Verified Software Update Pipelines
mitigations.description: Implement a robust OTA and service-update process that delivers timely security patches, verifies update integrity with digital signatures, and ensures all infotainment components—including third-party OS modules—receive consistent, OEM-controlled updates to eliminate known vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them.

mitigations.name: Hardening of Infotainment OS and Isolation From Critical Networks
mitigations.description: Reduce the attack surface of infotainment systems through OS hardening (service minimization, sandboxing, memory protections, privilege separation) and isolate them from safety-critical networks using secure gateways, preventing a compromised infotainment OS from executing arbitrary code that could pivot deeper into the vehicle.

mitigations.name: Implement Timely Patching
mitigations.description: Establish a robust patch management process to ensure timely updates for critical security components. Regularly monitor for vulnerabilities and apply patches immediately upon release. Prioritize patching based on severity and impact to maintain the integrity of your architecture.
mitigations.question: Is there a patch management process in place to apply critical security updates promptly based on severity and impact?
mitigations.consideration:

mitigations.description: Store all cryptographic keys, authentication tokens, and ECU credentials in hardware-backed secure elements or TPM-like modules, ensuring secrets are non-exportable, encrypted at rest, and never exposed directly in flash or RAM where chip-off or debug extraction attacks are possible.

mitigations.name: Locked-Down Debug/Programming Interfaces With Secure Access Controls
mitigations.description: Disable or tightly restrict JTAG, SWD, and other debug/programming interfaces on production ECUs, require authenticated and authorized service sessions for any access, and log all attempts, preventing attackers from extracting keys or internal secrets through physical probing or low-level diagnostic channels.

mitigations.name: Message Freshness Enforcement With Counters, Nonces, or Timestamps
mitigations.description: Introduce freshness checks at the secure gateway or ECU level—such as rolling counters, monotonic timestamps, or nonce-based challenges—so each CAN message is validated as “new” and any replayed or out-of-sequence frames are rejected before reaching critical modules.

mitigations.name: Secure Gateway Filtering With Context and Rate Validation
mitigations.description: Route CAN traffic through a secure gateway that enforces contextual validation (expected timing, message frequency, and ECU state), blocking messages that repeat too quickly or appear outside their normal operational window, preventing attackers from replaying captured commands like unlock or start signals.

mitigations.name: Cryptographically Signed Firmware and Secure Boot Enforcement
mitigations.description: Require all ECU firmware and OTA packages to be cryptographically signed by a trusted OEM key, verify signatures and version metadata before any update is applied, and enforce secure boot so only verified firmware images can execute, blocking unauthorized or tampered reflashes.

mitigations.name: Hardened Update and Diagnostic Access Controls
mitigations.description: Restrict access to diagnostic ports and OTA update interfaces with strong authentication, role-based permissions, and locked-down reprogramming modes, and log all reflashing events, preventing untrusted tools or actors from initiating firmware updates outside approved service and OEM processes.

mitigations.name: ECU Identity Verification With Message Authentication and Secure Gateways
mitigations.description: Require all CAN traffic to pass through a secure gateway that enforces message authentication (MACs, digital signatures, or link-layer authentication where supported) and validates sender identity against an authorized ECU list, ensuring forged or spoofed devices cannot masquerade as legitimate modules.

mitigations.name: Segmented Network Architecture With ECU Whitelisting and ID Filtering
mitigations.description: Isolate critical ECUs on protected CAN segments and enforce strict ID filtering and ECU whitelisting so only approved modules can transmit on specific message IDs or bus zones, preventing malicious devices from injecting spoofed control frames or responding on behalf of trusted ECUs.

mitigations.name: Memory-Safe Parsing, Bounds Enforcement, and Hardened Firmware Builds
mitigations.description: Use strict bounds checking, validated parsing routines, and safe memory-handling patterns in ECU firmware, combined with compiler hardening features (stack canaries, ASLR, DEP, and fortified libc) to prevent malformed CAN or diagnostic packets from triggering memory corruption or enabling arbitrary code execution.

mitigations.name: Input Validation and Gateway-Level Sanitization of Network Traffic
mitigations.description: Validate all inbound CAN, UDS, and diagnostic payloads at a secure gateway ECU, enforcing protocol correctness, length limits, and service-level restrictions so malformed or oversized packets never reach vulnerable modules, reducing exploitation opportunities against high-privilege ECU firmware.

mitigations.name: Rate-Limiting and Priority Enforcement at Secure Gateways
mitigations.description: Use a secure gateway ECU to enforce per-ID rate limits, validate arbitration priority usage, and drop frames that exceed allowable transmission frequency so attackers cannot monopolize CAN bandwidth or suppress legitimate safety-critical traffic.

mitigations.name: Segmented CAN Networks With DoS-Resilient Isolation
mitigations.description: Isolate safety-critical ECUs on protected CAN segments and use bus guardians or hardware firewalls to block excessive or malformed traffic from non-critical domains, ensuring essential control and sensor messages continue to flow even during a flooding attempt.

mitigations.name: Verified Boot With Hardware-Backed Root of Trust
mitigations.description: Enforce secure boot on all ECUs by establishing a hardware-backed root of trust that validates firmware signatures, version metadata, and integrity before execution, preventing any unsigned or tampered boot images from loading—even after reboots or power cycles.

mitigations.name: Locked-Down Bootloader Access and Controlled Update Paths
mitigations.description: Disable or restrict bootloader reprogramming interfaces, require authenticated flashing sessions through approved service tools, and log or alert on any bootloader access attempts, ensuring attackers cannot exploit open or poorly protected boot modes to install persistent malicious firmware.

mitigations.name: Hardened Gateway ECUs With Domain Isolation and Message Authentication
mitigations.description: Implement strict domain isolation within the central gateway and enforce message authentication, ID filtering, and policy-based routing so even if a non-critical domain is compromised, malicious traffic cannot be bridged or forwarded into safety-critical CAN segments.

mitigations.name: Secure Gateway Firmware, Access Controls, and Continuous Monitoring
mitigations.description: Protect the gateway ECU with signed firmware, locked-down diagnostic/update interfaces, and runtime monitoring of cross-domain traffic patterns, immediately blocking or alerting on anomalous bridging behaviors that could indicate compromise or lateral movement from infotainment or telematics systems.

mitigations.name: Access-Controlled Diagnostic Modes With Strong Authentication
mitigations.description: Restrict advanced UDS services (programming, memory access, configuration changes) to authenticated dealer tools or authorized service equipment, using secure challenge–response protocols and PINs/keys so attackers cannot invoke privileged diagnostic functions through OBD-II or remote gateways.

mitigations.name: Gateway-Level Filtering and Segmentation of Diagnostic Traffic
mitigations.description: Route all diagnostic requests through a secure, policy-enforcing gateway ECU that filters UDS/OBD-II commands, blocks high-risk services by default, and isolates telematics or infotainment domains from the internal vehicle networks, preventing remote or unauthorized diagnostic access from reaching critical ECUs.

mitigations.name: Rate-Limited, Authenticated Control Traffic Through a Secure Gateway
mitigations.description: Enforce message authentication, CAN ID whitelisting, and strict rate limits at the central secure gateway to prevent attackers from flooding the Engine ECU with spoofed or excessive control commands, ensuring the ECU cannot be overwhelmed into unsafe operating states.

mitigations.name: Engine Safety Limiters Enforced at Hardware and ECU Levels
mitigations.description: Implement hardware-level rev-limiters, temperature cutoffs, and fail-safe operating modes that cannot be overridden by CAN messages, ensuring protective shutdown systems remain functional even if the ECU is saturated or receiving malicious inputs.

mitigations.name: Secure Gateway Filtering With Safety-Critical Message Authentication
mitigations.description: Route all braking and safety-related CAN traffic through a hardened secure gateway that enforces message authentication, ID whitelisting, and rate limits, blocking spoofed or manipulated frames from suppressing brake commands or disabling airbag deployment logic.

mitigations.name: Hardware-Enforced Safety Overrides and Fail-Safe Operating Modes
mitigations.description: Implement hardware-level safety systems (independent brake actuators, backup crash sensors, and non-bypassable airbag initiation circuits) that continue functioning even if the CAN bus is compromised, ensuring braking and airbag activation cannot be disabled via network commands.

mitigations.name: Mandatory Firmware Lifecycle Management and Decommissioning
mitigations.description: Establish strict firmware lifecycle policies that require OEMs to maintain security updates for supported model years and explicitly decommission or block unsupported firmware from operating, ensuring outdated infotainment systems cannot remain in use with known exploitable vulnerabilities.

mitigations.name: Secure Gateway Isolation and Hardening of Legacy Components
mitigations.description: Isolate legacy or unpatched infotainment modules behind a secure gateway with restricted privileges, service minimization, and strict traffic filtering, preventing known-vulnerable components from reaching safety-critical networks or exposing exploitable surfaces to remote attackers.

mitigations.name: Sensor Fusion Validation and Secure ADAS Message Filtering
mitigations.description: Implement cross-sensor validation, plausibility checks, and CAN message filtering inside the ADAS ECU so spoofed or missing data (e.g., fake distance readings or lane markers) is detected and rejected, preventing manipulated sensor inputs from degrading lane-keeping or adaptive cruise control.

mitigations.name: Fail-Safe ADAS Modes With Redundant Perception Paths
mitigations.description: Provide redundant sensing (camera + radar + ultrasonic), enforce safe fallback behavior when perception degrades (e.g., disengage ACC, limit steering assistance), and isolate ADAS ECUs from untrusted network domains, ensuring assistance systems fail safely instead of applying unsafe control actions.
